title: Science and faith
hookLine: Muslims who see the study of nature as reading Allah's signs

lines: THE SKY, THE MOUNTAINS, THE EARTH.
cards: "Will they not regard the camels, how they are created?" A line of the Qur'an, in Pickthall's words, from surah al-Ghashiyah. It doesn't argue.
It points. And it keeps pointing: at the sky, how it is raised; at the mountains, how they are set; at the earth, how it is spread out.
A scripture that stops in the middle of its message to say: look at the animal in front of you, and ask how it was made. So what happens when a person of faith picks up a microscope?

teach.h: AYAH: A VERSE, AND A SIGN.
teach.b: Start with a word that does double duty. In the Qur'an, ayah, plural ayat, is used for the verses of the scripture, and also for signs in the world.
In surah Al 'Imran, in paraphrase, the creation of the heavens and the earth, and the alternation of night and day, are signs for people of understanding.
Some Muslim writers put it simply: there are two books, the book revealed and the book of creation, and both are read for signs. Then an invitation to look.
Beyond the camels, other verses point at rain, at bees, at the stages of a child in the womb, at the variety of languages and colors.
In Ibn Majah, in paraphrase, the Prophet, peace be upon him, calls seeking knowledge a duty on every Muslim. The history has practical roots.
Finding the qibla, the direction of prayer, and the times of the prayers took careful work with the sky.
Tradition remembers scholars like Ibn al-Haytham, who studied how light and sight work, and Ibn Sina, who wrote on medicine.
And the questions still open. Muslims today work across the sciences and discuss how faith and findings fit together. Some writers look for scientific wonders foretold in the Qur'an.
Other scholars caution against this, because science revises itself, and they'd rather not tie a verse to a theory that may change.
Some see no conflict to resolve at all: for them, studying a cell or a star is reading signs, and the reading itself is worship.

how: Muslims point to verses that call the creation of the heavens and earth, night and day, and living things signs, ayat, and to the hadith on seeking knowledge; Muslim scientists and scholars today discuss how findings and faith fit together, with some looking for scientific wonders in the Qur'an and others cautioning against it.

practice: Notice the breath itself: air moving in, the chest rising, something in you taking what it needs without being asked. Then look at your own hand for a moment, the creases, the joints, the way it closes.
If you pray, look at it the way the verse looks at the camel, and ask how it was made; if not, simply stay curious.

wordCard.voice: Science and faith. For Muslims who read the world as ayat, signs, studying nature is a way of reading the book of creation alongside the book revealed. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: a sign; in the Qur'an, both a verse of scripture and a sign in creation.

carryVoice: Your line: science reads signs. Two books, and both are read for signs. See you tomorrow.
